body.text: In July, Bengaluru cleared many footpaths under the “Safe Footpath Campaign”, with the worthy goal of enhanced pedestrian safety. This is a crucial issue for Bengaluru’s citizens as an estimated 300 pedestrians die in the city each year. Older people, children, and people with disabilities have an inalienable right to safe streets and footpaths.
The campaign’s goal was to remove unauthorised petty shops, pushcarts, commercial ramps, illegal extensions, and display boards that force pedestrians onto active vehicular lanes.

Yet, this campaign has evoked mixed public sentiment. Many praise the effort to make the city walkable and clear long-standing bottlenecks, while others voice scepticism about long-term enforcement patterns and livelihood impacts on vendors. Street vendor groups have strongly opposed the eviction methods adopted, staging massive protests, including a citywide bandh.

But the issue here is not about whether pedestrians or vendors have a stronger claim to footpaths. Both their claims are legitimate. The more pertinent question is why street markets, an urban provisioning system that serves between 1.4 million and 2 million Bengaluru citizens, are viewed by city authorities as encroachments to be removed.

Individual vendors when repeatedly clustered around particular places and flows of people collectively create street markets. Their stalls, which predictably appear in convenient locations, provide affordable fresh food and daily necessities to low-income households. Most street vendors are also subsistence vendors for whom this is the sole livelihood of their households, which have little buffer to absorb even a temporary loss of income.

City authorities, meanwhile, can only protect what they see. A road, a flyover, a market building, or a shopping complex is budgeted, constructed, and officially inaugurated. Street markets are different; they may appear accidental and disorganised. But they are functioning markets created through thousands of everyday vendor-customer transactions.

Street markets remain precarious because city authorities see a crowded pavement, a cart, a tarpaulin, discarded packaging, or customers spilling on the road. These are visible negative externalities, especially to drivers, pedestrians, formal shop owners, and the neighbourhood’s residents. What is not visible is how street markets are crucial provisioning systems for millions of low-income consumers.

Manual labourers can buy three tomatoes and a few green chillis for a meal, sometimes on credit until their weekly wages arrive. A supermarket or even the neighbourhood kirana shop may stock a wider range of standardised and perhaps even higher quality products. But for many low-income households, supermarkets cannot match what street markets provide: the ability to buy in tiny quantities from a stall very close to home and from vendors who know them well, even when cash is not available. Moreover, unbanked or less literate consumers may find street markets less intimidating and easier to navigate than formal retail.

A similar pattern of not counting street vendors exists across other cities in the Global South. Before the 2014 FIFA World Cup tournament in Rio de Janeiro, city authorities forcibly relocated street markets to distant sites to present international visitors with a clean image of the city. This permanently disrupted food access for thousands of low-income residents and destroyed vendors’ livelihoods. Bengaluru authorities, like others around the world, are counting what street markets obstruct but not what they provide.

The people served by street markets also typically have little political power. Their low-income customers and the street vendors themselves are not well-represented in business chambers and municipal committees. Hence, street vendors remain largely voiceless and are heard only when they collectively block a road or call for a bandh. Meanwhile, high-income residents who are likely to primarily experience street markets by their negative externalities have the social and political capital to influence the city’s decision-making.

India’s Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act of 2014 was passed to give street vendors a voice. This Act requires instituting Town Vending Committees with at least 40 per cent of its members representing street vendors. The goals of these committees include issuing vendor identity cards and vending certificates and proactively managing eviction and relocation.

Bengaluru did not have such a committee until the recent protests. It was only later that the Karnataka government announced a provisional Town Vending Committee and the issuance of identity cards for vendors.
It must be noted that vendor representation is meaningful only when it shapes decisions before sites are cleared.
The formalisation trap

The typical response of city authorities to conflicts over street vending is formalisation: register vendors, issue identity cards, designate vending zones, impose fixed hours, collect fees, or even relocate them to a new site, away from the current location.

Imposing these requirements negatively impacts the viability of street markets. Street markets function effectively because vendors follow customer foot traffic, flexibly vary their hours, and move between different locations. A vegetable seller who sets up a stall near a bus depot around the time workers return home in the evening serves customers where they most need it.

Relocation of street markets can destroy them. There may be fewer customers in the new market, leading some vendors to leave the market. Fewer vendors in a new market with a narrow product selection will then bring even fewer customers, so the new market will soon fail to thrive.

In 2019, Mexico City attempted to formalise its tianguis (weekly street markets) with itinerant vendors by offering them permits, fixed locations, and schedules. What this effort did not offer was mobility to these historically itinerant vendors. Now assigned to new fixed markets, they lost many of their customers and soon became unviable.

Bengaluru now confronts a version of the same issue. The government has explored relocation to fixed market sites as a response to conflicts over vending. One proposed site for a new market in Old Madras-Banaswadi Road Layout has generated opposition from residents concerned about congestion, waste, noise, and the area’s vulnerability to flooding. Strikingly, these are the same complaints that drove the clearance of the original street markets.
The problem is not whether and where vendors should be moved but how they can be accommodated without burdening them with the costs of relocation.
Protection without full formalisation
It is without question that Bengaluru has to ensure pedestrian safety. But it also has to recognise that its street markets are part of how the city feeds millions of its citizens. It can do both.

To start with, a focus on pedestrian safety must not penalise only street vendors. Parked vehicles, shop extensions, utility structures, and construction debris also obstruct pedestrians. A safety campaign where its most vulnerable citizens bear the highest costs is neither fair nor legitimate. Equitable urban design should create walk-only side streets, allow timed vending on some streets, and use common urban spaces such as parks to accommodate street vendors.

To be effective, Town Vending Committees must be set up before conflicts erupt. Vendor representatives, who have the best local market knowledge, should be enlisted to help authorities identify blocked pedestrian passages, time-sharing possibilities, and sites for pavement widening and to help assess relocation sites on an ongoing basis.

A provisioning system serving millions of citizens deserves the same scrutiny as that applied to infrastructure projects. City authorities should conduct a comprehensive audit of street markets. This audit should cover the number and types of vendors, the number of customers, the product categories, the transport connections to the area, the operating times, the neighbourhoods served, and the negative externalities, including noise, congestion, and waste. Clearing a street market should require both a vendor and a consumer impact assessment, just as infrastructure projects require all-around environmental impact assessments.

In this regard, cities should distinguish vendor registration from full formalisation. Vendor registration involves ensuring issuance of identity cards, basic health and sanitation standards, and access to waste disposal and fresh water, all provided without imposing the compliance costs of the formal sector on street vendors. This has worked well in Ahmedabad, where the Self-Employed Women’s Association reportedly provided identity cards to 13,000 street vendors with zero compliance costs.

Where relocation of a street market to another site is unavoidable, as it may well be in some cases, the new site must be assessed for customer foot traffic, transport access, customer potential, and vendor affordability. Following the move, vendor income and customer usage at the new market should be monitored and support provided, as needed, to ensure viability.

Treating street markets as an essential urban service does not mean their negative externalities can be overlooked. Vendors have a responsibility to ensure that the urban commons of footpaths are available for pedestrian use before and after market hours, even as their right to operate the street market is protected.

Bengaluru and other cities should clear their footpaths to improve pedestrian safety. But they should be careful not to clear away the street markets that make provisioning affordable and convenient for millions of its citizens. The challenge is to design a city that makes room for both.

Raji Srinivasan is a professor of marketing at the University of Texas at Austin, US. This article draws, in part, on research on tianguis conducted by the author with Maria Merino, a professor at Instituto Tecnológico Autónomo de México in Mexico City. The opinions expressed are those of the author.
